Now I have all the information I need. Let me compile the audit report:

## Audit Report: RR-MoA Paper Claims & Hedging Balance

### 1. ABSTRACT (exact text)

Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are deployed with frozen backbones and small per-task adapters: one TSFM can serve thousands of tenants through few-MB adapter weights (${\sim}1.7$\,MB on MOMENT-small) hot-swapped from host RAM in microseconds. Standard adapters use the same head for every window. Since real series mix heterogeneous regimes, a natural upgrade is a mixture of expert adapters that picks a different head per input window. We show this fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization once any backbone layers are unfrozen: routing entropy collapses to $0.000$ and all but one expert receive zero gradient. We call this *normalization-induced routing collapse*: the per-window mean and variance the router needs are stripped by RevIN, which is built into MOMENT and into any TSFM that adopts the same instance-normalization recipe. A $720$-run sweep across five standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recovers at most $10.9\%$ MSE, still $2.7\times$ worse than our fix, because the failure is in the router's input, not its optimization. We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor of when collapse matters (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$), correctly flagging boundary datasets where raw routing should not help. The fix follows: *Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters* (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. **RR-MoA wins $54/54$ dataset/freeze-level cells on the primary backbone ($27$--$77\%$ MSE improvement over the best fixed adapter), generalizes across four further backbones and an imputation task, and is isolated to instance normalization by eight causal controls including a vision modality.** The same principle predicts a *Frozen Paradox* we verify: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. Applying the same raw-signal principle at the expert level (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) closes the remaining gap to per-dataset supervised baselines.

---

### 2. CONTRIBUTIONS (all \item entries, exact text)

**Item 1:** We identify *normalization-induced routing collapse*, a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that is distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature, and isolate it through eight causal controls all consistent with normalization as the cause.

**Item 2:** We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) that yields a signal-ratio predictor of which datasets benefit from raw routing, including boundary cases where they do not, and validate the same principle across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.

**Item 3:** We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and a companion variant (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) that restores raw-signal access at the expert level. The non-triviality is not that raw access helps in the abstract, but *which* signal must be restored and *where*: naive $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection fails ($+42$--$239\%$ MSE; $11/18$ cells re-collapse), **standard rescue mechanisms that do not restore raw access fail ($720$ runs, $\leq 10.9\%$ recovery, $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA)**, and the signal-ratio predictor correctly flags datasets where raw routing should *not* help (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Together they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability.

---

### 3. CONCLUSION & LIMITATIONS (exact text)

**Opening claim:** MoE adapters on instance-normalized TSFMs fail for structural reasons: the normalization needed for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs. Raw pre-normalization routing fixes the failure and motivates Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}; $R(\mathcal{D})$ identifies where it applies.

**Implication paragraph:** Routing collapse on instance-normalized backbones illustrates a broader pattern: when a foundation model's input pipeline destroys signal a downstream router needs, optimization-side rescues (load balancing, z-loss, ReLU routing) cannot recover what is structurally absent --- **the fix is more readily approached by restoring the missing input than by retuning the optimizer.** The same mechanism appears in a vision control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); the signal-ratio predictor characterizes when raw-signal access should help in the regimes we tested.

**Limitations paragraph:** Three boundaries scope our claims. **(i) Normalization specificity.** Our diagnosis applies to backbones with instance-level normalization (RevIN, BatchNorm, GroupNorm); **backbones without it (Chronos, Timer-XL) show no collapse and no RR-MoA gain, as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts.** Extensions to attention-based or learned normalizers are not characterized. **(ii) Signal-ratio boundary cases.** The signal-ratio predictor $R(\mathcal{D})$ is a single monotone proxy for variance contribution; **on Solar ($R{=}0.06$) it correctly flags low benefit but is not sharp.** Datasets with strong shape-statistics coupling fall outside the tight regime of the bound. **(iii) Forecasting and imputation only.** We evaluate forecasting and imputation on LTSF benchmarks. Anomaly detection, classification, and irregularly-sampled tasks are deferred to future work.

---

| Phrase | Location | Context | Assessment |
|--------|----------|---------|------------|
| "only the scale-and-offset component" | Intro, p.66 | "instance normalization handles **only the scale-and-offset component of that heterogeneity**" | **Calibrated** — literally true; explicitly motivates why residual shape heterogeneity persists |
| "still underperforms" | Intro, p.68 | "Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing **still underperforms**" | **Appropriate** — quantified later (e.g., Table 1 shows 27–77% gains) |
| "does not help" | Intro, p.68 | "Standard MoE rescue mechanisms...also **do not help**" | **Strong claim, well-supported** — backed by 720-run sweep; best rescue recovers only 10.9% vs. 2.7× worse than RR-MoA |
| "partially recover" | Related Work, p.234 | "DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts}...**partially recover** stripped statistics" | **Appropriate** — distinguishes weaker baselines |
| "does not fully" (absence) | Not found | N/A | N/A |
| "is not sharp" | Conclusion, p.658 | "on Solar ($R{=}0.06$) it correctly flags low benefit **but is not sharp**" | **Appropriately hedged** — acknowledges Solar as outlier despite correct directional prediction |
| "not characterized" | Conclusion, p.658 | "Extensions to attention-based or learned normalizers **are not characterized**" | **Properly scoped** — honest boundary on scope |

**Key observation:** Hedges are *tightly scoped* to actual limitations (Solar outlier, Chronos/Timer-XL no-collapse negative controls). None contradict the core claims.

### 5. WIN-COUNT CLAIMS (counter-evidence: positive results)

| Claim | Location | Exact Quote | Raw Data Support |
|-------|----------|-------------|------------------|
| **54/54 RR-MoA wins** | Abstract, p.58 | "RR-MoA wins $54/54$ dataset/freeze-level cells on the primary backbone" | Table 1 (main results): 6 datasets × 3 freeze levels × 3 seeds = 54 configurations. All show RR-MoA > fixed adapter. MSE improvements: **27–77%**. |

Residual-IA⁺ achieves 107 match-or-beat with **65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1 ratio)**. Also: **6/6 at H=192**, **23/24 on MOMENT-Large (96%)**, **12/12 on Timer-XL (100%)**, **15/15 on Moirai-MoE (100%)**. |

Best (z-loss c_z=0.01): **10.9% recovery**. RR-MoA is **2.7× better**. Table S1 in appendix confirms complete sweep. |

## SUMMARY: ARE WE UNDERSELLING?

**Verdict: NO, you are not underselling after the hedging pass.** Here's why:

1. **Hedges are tightly scoped to reality:**
   - "not sharp" on Solar = true (R=0.06, still 32.9% improvement — outlier not invalidating the predictor's directional accuracy)

2. **Positive claims are unhedged and match data:**

3. **The diagnosis (core contribution) is stated boldly and correctly:**

We show this fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization once any backbone layers are unfrozen: routing entropy collapses to $0.000$ and all but one expert receive zero gradient. We call this *normalization-induced routing collapse*: the per-window mean and variance the router needs are stripped by RevIN, which is built into MOMENT and into any TSFM that adopts the same instance-normalization recipe. A $720$-run sweep across five standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recovers at most $10.9\%$ MSE, still $2.7\times$ worse than our fix, because the failure is in the router's input, not its optimization. 58:Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are deployed with frozen backbones and small per-task adapters: one TSFM can serve thousands of tenants through few-MB adapter weights (${\sim}1.7$\,MB on MOMENT-small) hot-swapped from host RAM in microseconds. Standard adapters use the same head for every window. Since real series mix heterogeneous regimes, a natural upgrade is a mixture of expert adapters that picks a different head per input window. We show this fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization once any backbone layers are unfrozen: routing entropy collapses to $0.000$ and all but one expert receive zero gradient. We call this \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: the per-window mean and variance the router needs are stripped by RevIN, which is built into MOMENT and into any TSFM that adopts the same instance-normalization recipe. A $720$-run sweep across five standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, expert-choice) recovers at most $10.9\%$ MSE, still $2.7\times$ worse than our fix, because the failure is in the router's input, not its optimization. RR-MoA wins $54/54$ dataset/freeze-level cells on the primary backbone ($27$--$77\%$ MSE improvement over the best fixed adapter), generalizes across four further backbones and an imputation task, and is isolated to instance normalization by eight causal controls including a vision modality. 64	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide powerful pretrained representations for time series, with several recent variants pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}. 1. **Title**: `"Diagnosis and a Minimal Fix"` — "Minimal" here is reading as small/marginal rather than "minimal causal intervention." Reviewers often parse "minimal fix" as "tweak."
2. **Contributions item 3 (line 76)**: `"a minimal architectural fix"` — same issue, plus the next sentence opens with `"The non-triviality is not that raw access helps in the abstract, but..."` which leads with the apologetic "non-triviality is not X" frame instead of asserting what *is* the contribution.
3. **Appendix line 2562**: `"pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix"` — defensive reframe inside the gap-closing reframing block.

The pattern: "minimal" is meant to convey "the smallest causal intervention that fixes the failure mode" (a strong claim — *no smaller change works*, evidenced by 720 runs of larger optimization-side fixes failing). But it reads as "small change, not much to see here."

**Two options for re-balancing:**

**Option A — replace "minimal" with the causal claim it stands for.**
- Title: `"...Diagnosis and a Causal Fix..."` or `"...Diagnosing and Fixing..."`
- Contributions: `"a single-input causal fix"` or `"the smallest input-level change that recovers routing"`
- Appendix: `"pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the causal fix at the router input"`

**Option B — keep "minimal" but pair it with the load-bearing evidence in the same sentence so the word reads as a claim, not a hedge.** E.g., contributions item 3 becomes:
> "We propose RR-MoA, the *minimal causal intervention* that fixes the collapse: changing only the router's input. Larger optimization-side interventions fail (720 runs, ≤10.9% recovery, 2.7× worse than RR-MoA), naive (μ,σ) re-injection fails (+42–239% MSE), and the signal-ratio predictor correctly flags where raw routing should not help (Traffic, R=0.14). Together with Residual-IA⁺, they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability."

Option B is closer to your existing text and only changes the framing verb. The "non-triviality is not X" opening goes away, replaced by an asserted claim ("the minimal causal intervention").

I'd recommend **Option B for the contributions bullet** (smallest diff, biggest tone shift) and **leaving the title alone** — "Minimal Fix" in titles is a common positive academic register (cf. "A Simple Framework for...", "The Minimum Description Length Principle"), and changing the title risks more than it gains this close to deadline.

lines: \textbf{Routing entropy diagnostics.} In all $30$ Raw-MLP MoE runs, routing entropy saturates near $\log K = 1.609$ (range $1.20$--$1.60$, mean $\approx 1.49$), indicating the router degenerates to near-uniform mixing. This means the Raw-MLP MoE is operating as a learned ensemble of $5$ size-diverse MLPs rather than as a per-sample mixture of specialists; the diversity comes from the heterogeneous expert capacities rather than from per-window routing decisions.

-\textbf{What this does and does not say about the paper's core claims.} This finding does \emph{not} undermine the central diagnosis of the paper: normalization-induced routing collapse on hidden-state routers (AdaMix) is a real, mechanistically-explained phenomenon that affects every TSFM with internal RevIN, and pre-normalization routing (RR-MoA) is the minimal fix. That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset: it would remain true if the TSFM were replaced by any other backbone with internal instance normalization. What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''

What this finding \emph{does} say is that the dual-stream gap-closing story should be reframed: rather than ``the TSFM has complementary nonlinear features that dual-stream extracts,'' the more accurate reading is ``the TSFM contributes complementary signal on datasets with nonlinear dynamics (where it wins by $1$--$6\%$), and contributes essentially nothing on datasets where DLinear is already near-optimal (where pure raw-MLP MoE matches or beats it).''

\textbf{Why we report this rather than hide it.} A pure raw-MLP MoE ablation was not in the original submission and was added in response to a reviewer who pointed out that, given Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}'s finding that the TSFM destroys nonlinear temporal structure, the obvious test of whether the TSFM is dead weight was missing. The reviewer's intuition was partially correct: the TSFM is dead weight on Weather, ETTm2, and Electricity, but not on the temperature-data datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1). We include the full result here because hiding it would invite the same attack at the next round of review, and because the dataset-conditional contribution of the TSFM is itself an interesting empirical pattern that deserves attention from the TSFM-design community. The honest takeaway: \emph{frozen TSFMs are useful where forecasting requires nonlinear temporal modeling beyond what a 5-MLP ensemble can express, and unnecessary where it does not}. The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone: it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.
